answers.text: Always give three lines, same order — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted. If there's no damage mentioned, write 'none' rather than leaving the line out.
List every call by time, customer, topic and outcome, then count how many need a follow-up at the bottom. If a customer calls twice in the same week, list both but only count the outcome once.
The finishing time doesn't add up — an 8am start for six hours wouldn't spill into the next day. I'd check the actual dates before filing.
96 to 118 looks like more than a 20% rise to me. The on-time rate might be worth double-checking too.
Output 2 — it shows the 940 and 827 behind the 88%. Output 1 could well be right too, but there's no way to check it without re-running the numbers.
Email 2 — it's got the actual volume figures, 1,200 to 1,650. Email 1 just says 'current volumes' without saying what that means, so there's nothing there to verify.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. Yes, it's already published on their site. 5. No.
I'd redact the hourly rates, and I'd flag the non-disclosure clause too since it names both parties.
I'd cross-check the stock counts against the system before the summary goes out.
Step 1 matters because a bad read carries through, but step 4 — the automatic submission — is where I'd really want the gate, since that's the point you can't undo.
